- Geometric Brownian motion $dS = \mu S\,dt + \sigma S\,dW$ gives $d(\ln S) = (\mu - \tfrac12\sigma^2)dt + \sigma\,dW$. That $-\sigma^2/2$ is why the **median** of a lognormal sits below its mean, and why the risk-neutral drift in Black-Scholes is $r - \sigma^2/2$ inside the log.

## Martingales in this setting
A process is a martingale exactly when its $dt$ term vanishes. So $W_t$ is, $W_t^2$ is not but $W_t^2 - t$ is, and $\exp(\sigma W_t - \tfrac12\sigma^2 t)$ is — the last one is the stochastic exponential and is the change-of-measure density in Girsanov.

## First passage time
Let $T_a$ be the first time $W$ hits level $a$. By the **reflection principle**, $P(\max_{s\le t} W_s \ge a) = 2P(W_t \ge a)$. Consequences: $P(T_a < \infty) = 1$ — you hit any level eventually — but $E[T_a] = \infty$. Certain, but not soon, and the density has such a fat tail that its mean diverges.

## Common mistakes
- Applying ordinary chain rule and losing the second-order term.
- Writing $\int W\,dW = W_T^2/2$.
- Saying "$W^2$ is a martingale because $E[W]=0$" — check the drift, not the mean.
- Confusing $E[T_a] = \infty$ with "it might never happen".

notes.title: Order Statistics
notes.body:
## Core idea
Order statistics are the sorted values $X_{(1)} \le \cdots \le X_{(n)}$ of a sample. The trick that makes almost every question easy: work with the **CDF of the max or min directly**, because "the max is below $x$" means "all of them are below $x$".

## When to use (trigger)
"Expected value of the maximum of $n$ draws", "distribution of the smallest", "expected range", "how are max and min correlated", "expected value of the $k$th largest".

## The two facts that do the work
For iid draws with CDF $F$:
- $P(X_{(n)} \le x) = F(x)^n$ — the max is below $x$ only if every draw is.
- $P(X_{(1)} > x) = (1 - F(x))^n$ — the min exceeds $x$ only if every draw does.

Everything else follows by differentiating or by the tail formula $E[X] = \int_0^\infty P(X>x)dx$.

## Uniform [0,1] results to memorise
- $E[X_{(k)}] = \dfrac{k}{n+1}$. The $n$ draws cut the interval into $n+1$ gaps of equal expected length.
- So $E[\max] = \dfrac{n}{n+1}$ and $E[\min] = \dfrac{1}{n+1}$.
- $X_{(k)} \sim \text{Beta}(k,\, n+1-k)$.
- $E[\text{range}] = \dfrac{n-1}{n+1}$.
- For $n=2$: $\operatorname{Corr}(\min,\max) = 1/2$.

The $k/(n+1)$ result is the same "equal expected gaps" symmetry behind the without-replacement shortcut — worth noticing, because it means one idea covers both topics.

## Exponentials
The minimum of independent $\text{Exp}(\lambda_i)$ is $\text{Exp}(\sum\lambda_i)$, and the probability that draw $i$ is the smallest is $\lambda_i/\sum\lambda_j$. This is the basis of competing-risks models and of simulating which of several Poisson events fires first.

## Common mistakes
- Integrating the joint density when the CDF route is one line.
- Assuming max and min are independent — they are positively correlated, and strongly so for small $n$.
- Answering $1/2$ for $E[\max]$ of two uniforms; it is $2/3$.
- Forgetting that these results assume **iid**; correlated draws change everything.

notes.title: Algorithms & Numerical Methods
notes.body:
## Core idea
Quant interviews ask algorithm questions to see whether you can find the **one pass** through the data instead of the obvious nested loop, and numerical questions to see whether you know when a method blows up.

## When to use (trigger)
"Do this in one pass", "what is the complexity", "how would you shuffle an array", "how many tests do you need to find the poisoned bottle", "how do you speed up this Monte Carlo", "is this scheme stable".

## The one-pass instinct
Most of these questions have an $O(n^2)$ answer you should mention and then improve on.
- **Maximum contiguous subarray**: Kadane's. Track the best sum ending here and the best seen anywhere; reset the running sum to zero whenever it goes negative. $O(n)$, $O(1)$ space.
- **The element appearing once** when all others appear twice: XOR everything. Equal values cancel, $O(n)$ time and no extra memory.
- **Polynomial evaluation**: Horner's rule, $((a_nx + a_{n-1})x + \cdots)$ — $n$ multiplications instead of $O(n^2)$, and numerically more stable.
- **Moving average**: keep a running sum, add the new point and subtract the one leaving. $O(1)$ per update.
- **Random permutation**: Fisher-Yates. For $i$ from $n-1$ down to 1, swap $a_i$ with a uniform index in $[0,i]$. The naive "swap each element with a uniformly random index in $[0,n-1]$" is **biased** — it generates $n^n$ equally likely execution paths, which cannot divide evenly into $n!$ permutations.

## Information-theoretic bounds
"1000 bottles, one poisoned, one test takes a day and you have one day — how many rats?" Each rat gives one bit, so $k$ rats distinguish $2^k$ cases and you need $2^k \ge 1000$, giving $k = 10$. Label the bottles in binary and have rat $i$ drink from every bottle whose $i$th bit is 1.

The same counting argument bounds comparison sorting at $\Omega(n\log n)$ — $n!$ outcomes need $\log_2(n!) \approx n\log_2 n$ binary comparisons. Reach for "how many bits does the answer need?" whenever a question asks for a minimum number of tests, weighings, or questions.

## Bit tricks
$n \,\&\, (n-1)$ clears the lowest set bit, so $n\,\&\,(n-1) = 0$ tests for a power of two. Multiplication by 7 is `(n<<3) - n`.

## Numerical methods
- **Monte Carlo** error falls as $1/\sqrt{N}$ — independent of dimension, which is exactly why it beats grids for high-dimensional payoffs. Variance reduction beats brute force: **antithetic variates** (use $Z$ and $-Z$), **control variates** (price something you know analytically alongside the target and correct by the known error), and **importance sampling** for rare events.
- **Finite difference**: the explicit scheme is easy but only conditionally stable, roughly requiring $\Delta t = O(\Delta x^2)$; implicit and Crank-Nicolson are unconditionally stable at the cost of solving a tridiagonal system per step. Crank-Nicolson is second-order accurate but can oscillate near a discontinuous payoff such as a digital.

## Common mistakes
- Giving the nested-loop answer and stopping.
- Quoting a complexity without saying what $n$ counts.
- Using the biased shuffle.
- Claiming Monte Carlo converges faster in low dimensions — the rate is always $1/\sqrt{N}$; what changes is what it is competing against.

notes.title: Modular Arithmetic & Number Theory
notes.body:
## Core idea
Working "mod $n$" means keeping only the remainder after dividing by $n$. It turns questions about infinitely many integers into questions about $n$ boxes — which is why it powers pigeonhole arguments, invariants, and every "can this state ever be reached" puzzle.

## When to use (trigger)
"Prove this is impossible", "what is the last digit of...", "show two of these have a difference divisible by...", "can the counts ever all be equal", anything about parity, divisibility, or remainders.

## The rules
Congruence $a \equiv b \pmod n$ means $n$ divides $a - b$. Arithmetic passes straight through:
$$a \equiv b,\ c \equiv d \implies a+c \equiv b+d, \quad ac \equiv bd \pmod n$$
Addition, subtraction and multiplication are safe. **Division is not** — you may only cancel $k$ when $\gcd(k,n)=1$.

## Parity is the case $n = 2$
Most invariant puzzles are just parity in disguise. Ask: does each move flip the quantity or preserve it? If a move always changes a count by 2, its parity is conserved forever, and any target with the wrong parity is unreachable. The 7-coins-in-a-circle problem, the mutilated chessboard, and the 15-puzzle are all this argument.

## Invariants modulo n
The general recipe for "can I get from state A to state B":
1. Find a quantity that every legal move changes in a **predictable** way modulo $n$.
2. Compute it for the start and for the target.
3. If they differ, no sequence of moves works — however long.

Chameleon colours are the classic: each meeting changes all three counts by $-1$ modulo 3, so the pairwise **differences** of the counts are invariant mod 3. Start at residues $(1,0,2)$ — all different — and a monochromatic state needs $(0,0,0)$. Unreachable, proved in three lines.

## Facts worth carrying
- **Divisibility by 9** (and 3): a number is congruent to its digit sum mod 9, because $10 \equiv 1 \pmod 9$. Same trick gives the alternating-digit-sum rule for 11, since $10 \equiv -1 \pmod{11}$.
- **Last digit** of $a^k$ cycles with period dividing 4. $7^{100}$: the cycle is 7, 9, 3, 1, and $100 \equiv 0 \pmod 4$, so the last digit is 1.
- **Fermat's little theorem**: $a^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod p$ for prime $p$ not dividing $a$.
- **Trailing zeros of $n!$**: count factors of 5 (they are scarcer than 2s) via $\sum_k \lfloor n/5^k \rfloor$.
- **Residue classes as pigeonholes**: any $n+1$ integers contain two whose difference is divisible by $n$.
- **Bézout / gcd**: you can measure exactly $d$ litres with jugs of size $a$ and $b$ if and only if $\gcd(a,b)$ divides $d$.

## Common mistakes
- Dividing both sides of a congruence when the divisor shares a factor with the modulus.
- Choosing a modulus that does not actually separate the start from the target — if the invariant matches, you have learned nothing and must try another $n$ (2, 3 and 9 are the usual suspects).
- Proving a quantity is invariant for *some* moves and forgetting to check the rest.
- Treating an invariant argument as evidence rather than proof: it is a proof, and you should say so.

notes.title: Proof Techniques: Induction, Contradiction, Invariants
notes.body:
## Core idea
Some interview questions ask you to **prove** rather than compute. There is a small toolkit that covers nearly all of them, and knowing which tool a question wants is most of the battle — "show that", "prove", "is it possible" and "what is the minimum" each point at a different one.

## When to use (trigger)
"Prove that at least two...", "show this is always true", "is it possible to reach...", "what is the minimum number of moves", "show there are infinitely many...".

## Which tool for which question
| Phrasing | Reach for |
| --- | --- |
| "prove for all $n$" | induction |
| "prove this is impossible" | invariant, or contradiction |
| "show at least two share..." | pigeonhole |
| "what is the minimum number of steps" | a per-step invariant, then a construction |
| "show there are infinitely many" | contradiction (assume finitely many) |

## Induction
Prove the base case, then assume the statement for $n$ and derive it for $n+1$. **Strong induction** assumes it for all values up to $n$, which is what you need when the step splits the problem into two smaller pieces of unpredictable size — the chocolate-bar and coin-split problems both need it.

The commonest failure is a base case that does not actually anchor the chain, or an inductive step that quietly assumes the thing being proved.

## Proof by contradiction
Assume the negation, derive something impossible. Euclid's proof that primes are infinite is the model: assume finitely many, multiply them all and add 1, and you have a number divisible by none of them. Erdős–Szekeres works the same way — assume no long monotone subsequence, and the pigeonhole count immediately contradicts it.

## Invariants and monovariants
An **invariant** never changes; a **monovariant** only moves one way. Both settle "is this reachable" and "how many steps" questions instantly.

- *Invariant*: a chocolate bar's piece count rises by exactly 1 per break, so $mn$ squares always take $mn-1$ breaks — no strategy exists to beat it, and none is needed. Same argument gives $n-1$ matches in a knockout tournament.
- *Monovariant*: if a quantity strictly decreases and is bounded below, the process must terminate. That is how you prove a sorting or rearrangement game always ends.

## Counting and information bounds
The most underrated tool. To lower-bound the number of tests, weighings or questions, count how much **information** each one yields:
- Each yes/no answer is 1 bit, so $k$ of them distinguish at most $2^k$ cases. 1000 bottles with one poisoned needs $2^k \ge 1000$, so $k = 10$ rats.
- Each balance weighing has **three** outcomes, so $k$ weighings distinguish $3^k$. Twelve balls of unknown heavy-or-light is 24 cases, and $3^3 = 27 \ge 24$, so three weighings *might* suffice — and that tightness tells you every weighing must be near-maximally informative, which rules out timid opening moves.
- Comparison sorting must distinguish $n!$ orderings, giving the $\Omega(n\log n)$ bound.

Do this **before** searching for a procedure. It tells you what to aim for and whether to stop looking.

## Extremal principle
Consider the largest, smallest, or most extreme object. "Take the person who shook the most hands", "consider the shortest path" — the extreme case often forces the contradiction or the construction you need.

## A complete answer has two halves
For a minimum-$k$ question, you need a **lower bound** (a counting or invariant argument showing fewer is impossible) *and* a **construction** (an explicit method achieving it). Giving only one is a half-answer, and interviewers push on whichever you skipped. Where the bound is tight, showing that $k-1$ fails is what proves you understood it.

## Common mistakes
- Giving a construction and calling it a proof of minimality.
- Assuming the thing you are proving inside the inductive step.
- Answering a "prove" question with a probability — pigeonhole and invariants give certainty, not likelihood.
- Searching for a clever strategy when an invariant shows the answer is forced and no strategy exists.

notes.title: Interest Rate Risk Management
notes.body:
## Core idea
Instrument-level bond maths (duration, convexity) tells you how one bond moves. **Managing** rate risk is about a whole book exposed to a curve that does not move in parallel — which is why desks work in bucketed DV01s and principal components rather than a single duration number.

## When to use (trigger)
"How do you hedge a rates book", "what are the three principal components of the yield curve", "duration is not enough — why", "what is a key-rate duration", "how does a bank manage net interest income".

## Net interest income
A bank borrows short and lends long. If rates rise, funding reprices faster than assets and NII is squeezed. The classic mismatch: five-year fixed mortgages funded by overnight deposits. Managing it means either matching repricing dates, or accepting the mismatch and hedging with swaps. Note the **embedded optionality** that makes this hard — depositors withdraw and borrowers prepay precisely when it hurts, so the effective duration of both sides is state-dependent.

## Why a single duration is not enough
Duration assumes a **parallel shift**. Real curves steepen, flatten and twist, and a book that is duration-neutral can still lose heavily on a twist. Two responses:

**Bucketed / key-rate deltas.** Shift each part of the curve (1y, 2y, 5y, 10y, 30y) by one basis point separately and record the P&L. That vector is your actual exposure; the sum is the parallel DV01. Hedge bucket by bucket.

**Principal components.** Diagonalise the covariance matrix of rate changes. Empirically, three factors explain over 90% of yield curve variation:
1. **Level** (~80–90%) — all rates move together; this is what duration captures.
2. **Slope** (~5–10%) — short and long ends move oppositely.
3. **Curvature** (~1–2%) — the belly moves against the wings.

Express the book's exposure as sensitivity to those three factors instead of to 20 correlated tenors. Far fewer numbers, and they are uncorrelated by construction, so their risks add in quadrature.

## Gamma and vega for rates
Rate books have convexity (gamma) too, and it is the same trade-off as in equity options: positive convexity is paid for. Vega matters because caps, floors and swaptions are everywhere in a bank's balance sheet, often embedded rather than explicit.

## Common mistakes
- Reporting one duration for a book and calling it hedged.
- Adding percentage durations across positions — only **dollar** duration (DV01) adds.
- Treating a PCA hedge as exact: it is a three-factor approximation and leaves residual basis risk.
- Ignoring the optionality in deposits and prepayable loans, which is where the convexity actually lives.

notes.title: Correlations & Copulas
notes.body:
## Core idea
Correlation only captures **linear** dependence, and only fully describes a joint distribution when the marginals are normal. A copula separates the two questions — what each variable looks like on its own, and how they move together — which is what you need when the marginals are fat-tailed and the dependence lives in the tails.

## When to use (trigger)
"How do you monitor correlation", "what is a copula", "why did the Gaussian copula fail", "what is tail dependence", "two assets are uncorrelated — are they independent".

## Monitoring correlation
Update covariances the same way you update variances:
- **EWMA**: $\text{cov}_n = \lambda\,\text{cov}_{n-1} + (1-\lambda)x_{n-1}y_{n-1}$
- **GARCH**: add a long-run covariance term so forecasts mean-revert.

Correlation is then $\text{cov}/(\sigma_x\sigma_y)$ with each variance updated the same way. **Consistency matters**: if you update variances and covariances with different schemes, the resulting matrix can fail to be positive semidefinite, and then some portfolio has negative variance. Use the same $\lambda$ throughout.

## Correlation is not dependence
- $\rho = 0$ does **not** imply independence. $Y = X^2$ with $X$ symmetric has zero correlation and total dependence.
- Correlation is not invariant to nonlinear transformations — $\text{corr}(X,Y)$ and $\text{corr}(\ln X,\ln Y)$ differ.
- Two variables with given marginals cannot always attain a given $\rho$; the attainable range depends on the marginals.

## Copulas
Take each variable's marginal distribution, map it to a uniform via its own CDF (the **probability integral transform**), then map that to a standard normal. Now impose a correlation structure on the transformed variables. That correlation structure is the copula, and it is defined entirely separately from the marginals.

- **Gaussian copula**: transform to normals, impose a normal correlation matrix. Easy, and it has **zero tail dependence** — extreme moves become asymptotically independent.
- **Student-t copula**: same idea with a multivariate $t$. Has genuine tail dependence, so extremes co-occur. Almost always the better choice for risk.
- **Factor copula**: make each transformed variable $a_iF + \sqrt{1-a_i^2}Z_i$ with a single common factor $F$. Reduces $n(n-1)/2$ correlations to $n$ loadings and is what makes large portfolios tractable.

**Tail dependence** is the whole point: $\lim_{u\to 1}P(V_2 > u \mid V_1 > u)$. Zero for the Gaussian copula, positive for the $t$. Getting this wrong is what made the Gaussian copula infamous — it priced tranches as if extreme joint defaults were far rarer than they were, and calibrating it to benign data made the correlation input look reassuring.

## Vasicek's model
The single-factor Gaussian copula applied to loan defaults, giving the Basel capital formula: the worst-case default rate at confidence $X$ is $N\!\left(\frac{N^{-1}(\text{PD}) + \sqrt{\rho}\,N^{-1}(X)}{\sqrt{1-\rho}}\right)$.

## Common mistakes
- Treating uncorrelated as independent.
- Estimating correlations in calm markets and assuming they hold in stress — they rise toward 1 exactly when diversification was supposed to help.
- Using a Gaussian copula for anything where joint extremes matter.
- Building a correlation matrix pairwise and never checking it is positive semidefinite.

notes.title: Historical Simulation & Extreme Value Theory
notes.body:
## Core idea
Historical simulation makes no distributional assumption — which is its strength and its weakness. It cannot say anything about a loss bigger than the worst day in your window. **EVT** fixes exactly that: it fits a parametric tail so you can extrapolate beyond the observed data.

## When to use (trigger)
"How does historical simulation work", "what is its main weakness", "how do you compute a confidence interval for VaR", "what is EVT and why use it", "the power law".

## The methodology
Take $n$ days of history (typically 500). For each day, apply that day's **percentage** changes in every risk factor to today's portfolio, giving $n$ hypothetical P&Ls. Sort them; the 1% quantile is your 99% VaR. Note you are revaluing *today's* portfolio under *past* market moves — you are not looking up past P&L.

## Accuracy
The quantile estimate has real sampling error. The standard error of the $q$-quantile estimate is
$$\frac{1}{f(x)}\sqrt{\frac{q(1-q)}{n}}$$
where $f$ is the density at the quantile. Because $f$ is small in the tail, the error is large — a 99% VaR from 500 days routinely carries a standard error of several percent of the estimate. **Quote VaR with a confidence interval**, or at least know it is not a precise number.

## Extensions worth naming
- **Weighting by recency (BRW)**: give day $i$ weight $\propto \lambda^{i}$ so recent data counts more. Fixes the equal-weighting pathology where a big old return drops out of the window and VaR jumps for no reason.
- **Volatility scaling (Hull–White)**: rescale each historical return by $\sigma_{\text{today}}/\sigma_{\text{then}}$. This is the more important extension — it lets a calm-period window still produce a large VaR when current volatility is high.
- **Bootstrap**: resample the $n$ scenarios with replacement many times to get a confidence interval for VaR directly.

## Extreme value theory
The key result (Gnedenko / Pickands–Balkema–de Haan): for almost any parent distribution, the excess over a high threshold $u$ converges to a **generalised Pareto distribution**:
$$P(v > u + y \mid v > u) = \left(1 + \frac{\xi y}{\beta}\right)^{-1/\xi}$$
Two parameters: $\xi$ is the **shape** (tail heaviness) and $\beta$ the scale, fitted by maximum likelihood to the exceedances.

- $\xi > 0$ is the heavy-tailed (Fréchet) case — this is what financial returns show, typically $\xi \approx 0.1$–$0.4$.
- $\xi = 0$ gives an exponential tail (normal-like).
- Moments above $1/\xi$ do not exist, so $\xi > 0.5$ means infinite variance.

**Why it matters**: EVT lets you estimate a 99.9% VaR from 500 days of data, which raw historical simulation simply cannot do — the empirical quantile does not exist beyond the worst observation. It also smooths the tail rather than letting one outlier dictate the answer.

The **power law** is the same idea stated loosely: $P(v > x) = Kx^{-\alpha}$ for large $x$, with $\alpha = 1/\xi$. Plot $\ln P(v>x)$ against $\ln x$ and a straight line confirms it.

## Choosing the threshold
The bias–variance trade-off in one decision: too low and the GPD approximation is poor; too high and you have too few exceedances to fit. Rule of thumb is around the 95th percentile, and you should check the estimate is stable across nearby thresholds.

## Common mistakes
- Believing historical simulation is assumption-free — it assumes the past window represents the future.
- Reporting VaR to three significant figures when the standard error is 5%.
- Using EVT without checking the threshold choice.
- Forgetting that EVT models the **tail only**, not the whole distribution.

notes.title: The Model-Building Approach to VaR
notes.body:
## Core idea
Instead of replaying history, assume a distribution for the risk factors and propagate it analytically through the portfolio. Fast and it gives clean marginal risk numbers — but it needs the portfolio to be roughly **linear** in the risk factors, and options are not.

## When to use (trigger)
"Walk me through the variance–covariance approach", "how do you handle options in a parametric VaR", "what is delta–gamma", "cash-flow mapping", "model-building versus historical simulation".

## The linear model
For a portfolio with exposures $\alpha_i$ to risk factors with covariance $\Sigma$:
$$\sigma_P^2 = \alpha^\top \Sigma\, \alpha, \qquad \text{VaR} = z\,\sigma_P\sqrt{T}$$
With two assets this is the familiar $\sigma_P^2 = \alpha_1^2\sigma_1^2 + \alpha_2^2\sigma_2^2 + 2\rho\alpha_1\alpha_2\sigma_1\sigma_2$.

## Cash-flow mapping
A bond's cash flows land on arbitrary dates, but you only hold covariances for standard tenors. Map each cash flow onto the two adjacent standard vertices, choosing the split so that **present value and variance are both preserved**. That is the RiskMetrics construction, and getting the variance-preservation condition right is the part interviewers probe.

## Options: the delta approximation
$\Delta P \approx \delta\,\Delta S$, so treat the option as $\delta S$ worth of the underlying and run the linear model. Fast, and wrong in a specific direction: it ignores gamma, so it **understates** risk for a short-option book and misprices the asymmetry for a long one. A delta-neutral option book has *zero* VaR under the linear model, which is plainly false.

## The quadratic model (delta–gamma)
Add the second-order term:
$$\Delta P \approx \delta\,\Delta S + \tfrac12\gamma(\Delta S)^2$$
Now $\Delta P$ is no longer normal even if $\Delta S$ is — it is a quadratic form in normals, which is skewed. Handle it with a **Cornish–Fisher expansion**, which adjusts the normal quantile for skewness, or give up and simulate.

## Monte Carlo
Sample risk factors from the assumed multivariate distribution (Cholesky the covariance matrix), fully revalue the portfolio on each draw, and read the quantile. Handles arbitrary nonlinearity at the cost of one full revaluation per path — which is why banks use partial revaluation or grids for large books.

## Model-building vs historical simulation
| | Model-building | Historical simulation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Distribution | assumed (usually normal) | empirical |
| Fat tails | missed unless you add them | captured if in the window |
| Nonlinearity | needs delta–gamma or MC | exact, by revaluation |
| Speed | very fast | slower |
| Marginal/component VaR | analytic and clean | awkward |
| Correlations | must be estimated | implicit in the data |

Most banks run historical simulation for the headline number and the model-building approach for risk **attribution**, because the analytic form gives marginal and component VaR almost for free.

## Common mistakes
- Applying the linear model to an option book without mentioning gamma.
- Forgetting that $\Delta P$ stops being normal once the quadratic term is in.
- Assuming a normal distribution for daily returns when kurtosis is routinely 5–10.
- Mapping cash flows preserving PV but not variance.

notes.title: Basel & the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
notes.body:
## Core idea
Market risk capital rules are a direct response to what broke last time. Knowing *why* each change was made is far more useful in an interview than reciting the acronyms.

## When to use (trigger)
"Walk me through Basel", "what did FRTB change and why", "what is stressed VaR", "why did they move from VaR to ES", "trading book versus banking book".

## The sequence, and what each fixed
- **Basel I (1988)** — crude risk weights for credit, no market risk at all.
- **1996 Amendment** — introduced market risk capital, and with it the internal-models approach: 10-day 99% VaR, multiplied by at least 3, with the multiplier rising on backtesting exceptions (the traffic-light system: green 0–4, yellow 5–9 with escalating multiplier, red 10+).
- **Basel II (2004)** — three pillars; far more risk-sensitive credit treatment (IRB, based on Vasicek's model).
- **Basel II.5 (2009)** — the crisis response for the trading book: **stressed VaR** (the same calculation calibrated to a 12-month stressed period, added to ordinary VaR), the **incremental risk charge** for default and migration risk, and the comprehensive risk measure for correlation trading. Roughly tripled trading-book capital.
- **Basel III (2010–)** — more and better capital (CET1, buffers), plus a **leverage ratio** as a non-risk-based backstop, and two liquidity ratios: **LCR** (survive 30 days of stress) and **NSFR** (stable funding over a year).
- **FRTB (2016/2019)** — the full rebuild of market risk capital.

## FRTB: the four changes that matter
1. **ES at 97.5% replaces VaR at 99%.** ES is subadditive, and it sees the shape of the tail rather than a single quantile — so selling deep out-of-the-money options no longer looks free. The 97.5% level is chosen so that under normality it roughly matches a 99% VaR, keeping calibration familiar.
2. **Liquidity horizons.** Different risk factors get different holding periods (10 to 120 days) instead of a blanket 10-day assumption with $\sqrt{t}$ scaling. Recognises that you cannot exit an exotic credit position in two weeks.
3. **A hard trading/banking book boundary.** Pre-crisis, banks arbitraged the boundary by parking positions wherever capital was cheaper. FRTB makes reassignment very difficult and presumptive by instrument type.
4. **Desk-level model approval, with two tests.** A desk must pass the **P&L attribution test** (risk-model P&L must track actual P&L closely) and **backtesting**, or it falls back to the standardised approach for that desk. Plus **non-modellable risk factors** — factors without enough real observed prices get a punitive stressed capital add-on rather than model treatment.

## Common mistakes
- Reciting the timeline without saying what each change was responding to.
- Saying ES replaced VaR "because it is better" without naming subadditivity and tail-sensitivity.
- Forgetting that stressed VaR is *added to*, not instead of, ordinary VaR.
- Not knowing the P&L attribution test — it is the most commonly asked FRTB detail because it is the one that actually bites desks.

## Note
For a market risk role this is the regulatory spine of the job. Being able to explain the *motivation* for FRTB, not just its content, is what separates a candidate who has read about it from one who has worked with it.

notes.title: Counterparty Risk, Margin & CCPs
notes.body:
## Core idea
A derivative's value changes over its life, so your exposure to the counterparty is **stochastic** — you cannot know it up front. Margin, netting and clearing exist to cap it; CVA prices what remains.

## When to use (trigger)
"How does initial margin differ from variation margin", "what does a CCP actually do", "what is CVA", "wrong-way risk", "how is initial margin calculated".

## Margin
- **Variation margin** settles the *current* mark-to-market, usually daily (often intraday). It removes accumulated exposure, so it is about what has already happened.
- **Initial margin** covers *potential future* exposure over the close-out period — how much the position could move between the counterparty's last payment and your liquidation of the hedge. It is about what might happen next, and unlike VM it is not returned as the trade moves.
- Sizing IM: exchanges historically used **SPAN** (scenario grids over price and vol); modern CCPs mostly use a **VaR or ES model** over a 2–5 day close-out with a stressed lookback. Cleared OTC rates typically use a 5-day horizon; bilateral uncleared IM (under UMR) uses 10 days, commonly via the industry SIMM model.
- Margin is **procyclical** — a volatility spike raises IM exactly when funding is hardest. That is the central criticism of clearing and the reason anti-procyclicality floors exist.

## CCPs
A central counterparty novates each trade, becoming buyer to every seller and seller to every buyer. Benefits: multilateral netting, mutualised default management, transparency, and a standardised default waterfall. Costs: concentration of risk into a systemically critical node, and mandatory margin that consumes liquidity.

**The default waterfall**, in order: the defaulter's IM, then the defaulter's default-fund contribution, then the CCP's own "skin in the game", then the surviving members' default fund, then assessment rights on survivors. Knowing the order — and that surviving members are mutualised into losses — is the point of the question.

## Bilateral OTC
**Netting** under an ISDA master agreement means exposure is on the net portfolio, not trade by trade — which is why netting sets can cut exposure by an order of magnitude. **CSAs** govern collateral: threshold, minimum transfer amount, eligible collateral, haircuts.

## CVA and the XVA family
- **CVA**: the market value of counterparty default risk — expected loss from their default, computed as $\text{LGD}\times\int \text{EE}(t)\,\text{PD}(t)\,\text{d}f(t)$ over the exposure profile. It is a **charge against the derivative's value**, and it moves with credit spreads, which is why CVA desks hedge it and why CVA volatility is itself a market risk.
- **DVA**: the mirror image — your own default risk, which paradoxically produces a *gain* when your credit deteriorates.
- **FVA**: the funding cost of uncollateralised positions.

Exposure metrics: **EE** (expected exposure), **PFE** (potential future exposure, a high quantile of exposure at a horizon), **EPE** (time-averaged EE).

## Wrong-way risk
Exposure and counterparty credit quality are adversely correlated — you are owed most exactly when they are least able to pay. Classic case: buying protection on a sovereign from a bank domiciled in that sovereign. Right-way risk is the benign opposite. Independence between exposure and default is the convenient assumption in the CVA integral and it is often the wrong one.

## Common mistakes
- Conflating IM (future exposure) with VM (current exposure).
- Saying CCPs eliminate counterparty risk — they concentrate and mutualise it.
- Forgetting DVA exists, or failing to explain why booking a gain on your own credit deterioration is uncomfortable.
- Ignoring procyclicality when discussing margin.

## Note
Your clearinghouse work sits exactly here — the margin-model and waterfall material is the part to be able to speak to concretely.

notes.title: Scenario Analysis & Stress Testing
notes.body:
## Core idea
VaR and ES are calibrated to the recent past and to a probability model. Stress testing asks a different question — *what would happen if...* — with no probability attached. The two are complements, not substitutes, and the honest framing is that stress testing exists because your VaR model's assumptions will fail.

## When to use (trigger)
"How is stress testing different from VaR", "how do you choose scenarios", "what is reverse stress testing", "what do you do with the results", "CCAR / EBA stress tests".

## Generating scenarios
1. **Historical replay** — 1987, 1998 (LTCM), 2008, the 2010 flash crash, 2020 COVID, 2022 gilt/LDI. Defensible and easy to explain to a board, but limited to what has already happened.
2. **Hypothetical / expert judgement** — a risk committee posits a plausible shock. Flexible, forward-looking, but subjective and prone to missing what nobody thought of.
3. **Model-driven** — stress one factor and use the covariance matrix to imply consistent moves in the rest (conditional expectation given the shocked factor). Keeps scenarios internally coherent, but inherits the correlation assumptions that stress testing was supposed to escape.
4. **Reverse stress testing** — start from the outcome ("what kills us?") and work backwards to the scenarios that produce it. Regulators increasingly require this, and it is the most useful of the four because it surfaces exposures nobody had thought to test.

A good scenario is **severe, plausible, and internally consistent**. Shocking equities down 30% while leaving credit spreads unchanged is not a scenario, it is an arithmetic error.

## Regulation
**CCAR / DFAST** (US) and the **EBA/ECB** exercises (EU) impose supervisor-defined macro scenarios and require banks to project capital ratios through them. These are *capital-planning* exercises with real consequences — a failure can block dividends and buybacks — so they drive genuine business decisions rather than being a reporting formality.

## What to do with the results
This is where most candidates are weak. A stress number with no action attached is worthless. The uses are:
- **Limits** — set them on stressed losses, not just VaR.
- **Capital planning** — does the firm survive with capital above minimum?
- **Identifying concentrations** — which single scenario dominates the loss? That is your real exposure.
- **Contingency planning** — pre-agree what you would *do*: which positions to cut, in what order, and whether they are liquid enough to cut at all.

Assigning subjective probabilities to scenarios lets you combine stress results with VaR into a single loss distribution — Hull's suggestion, and a good answer to "how do you reconcile the two numbers".

## Common mistakes
- Treating stress testing as a regulatory box-tick rather than a risk tool.
- Scenarios that are severe but not coherent across asset classes.
- Only replaying history — the next crisis is not in your dataset.
- Producing results with no linked management action.

notes.title: Liquidity Risk
notes.body:
## Core idea
Two distinct risks share the name. **Trading (market) liquidity** is not being able to exit a position at the marked price. **Funding liquidity** is not being able to meet cash obligations. Both kill firms that were solvent on paper — Northern Rock and Lehman were funding failures, LTCM was a trading-liquidity failure.

## When to use (trigger)
"What is liquidity risk", "how do you adjust VaR for liquidity", "what is a liquidity black hole", "LCR and NSFR", "why did a solvent firm fail".

## Trading liquidity
Cost of unwinding is roughly half the bid–ask spread times position value, per position:
$$\text{cost} = \tfrac12 \sum_i s_i \alpha_i$$
where $s_i$ is the proportional spread. In stress, spreads widen, so a useful refinement is to use $\mu_i + \lambda\sigma_i$ in place of $s_i$, where $\sigma_i$ is the spread's own volatility — a stressed-spread liquidity adjustment.

**Liquidity-adjusted VaR** adds this unwind cost to ordinary VaR. The deeper problem is that VaR assumes you can exit within the horizon at marked prices, which is exactly false in stress — this is why FRTB replaced the blanket 10-day assumption with risk-factor-specific **liquidity horizons** of 10 to 120 days.

Position size relative to average daily volume is the practical metric: a position that is 20 days of ADV cannot be liquidated in a 10-day horizon at anything like the screen price.

## Funding liquidity
Failures come from maturity transformation plus a loss of confidence: short-term wholesale funding that does not roll, a ratings trigger, or margin calls in size. Basel III's two ratios respond directly:
- **LCR** — high-quality liquid assets must cover 30 days of stressed net outflows.
- **NSFR** — available stable funding must cover required stable funding over one year.

## Liquidity black holes
The self-reinforcing spiral: prices fall → margin calls and risk limits bind → forced selling → prices fall further. What makes it vicious is that **positive-feedback traders** (stop-losses, dynamic hedgers replicating options, margin-constrained leveraged funds, and portfolio insurers) all sell into declines by construction, so the usual stabilising negative-feedback flow disappears exactly when it is needed.

This is why **crowded trades** are dangerous even when each participant is individually well hedged: everyone's exit is the same door. And it is why correlations go to 1 in a crisis — the selling is driven by funding, not by fundamentals, so it hits everything at once.

## Common mistakes
- Conflating the two kinds of liquidity risk — say which one you mean.
- Assuming a position can be exited at mid.
- Modelling liquidity as a constant spread when it is precisely the thing that evaporates in stress.
- Describing a black hole as irrational — the individual behaviour is usually rational and mandated; the aggregate outcome is the problem.

notes.title: Model Risk
notes.body:
## Core idea
Every number on a risk report came out of a model, and every model is wrong in some specific way. Model risk is the risk of loss from using one anyway — through a wrong specification, wrong calibration, wrong implementation, or right model used for the wrong thing.

## When to use (trigger)
"What is model risk", "how do you validate a model", "why is Black–Scholes still used when its assumptions are false", "how would you detect a model problem", "physics versus finance".

## Where models sit on a spectrum
- **Linear products** (forwards, futures, swaps) — priced by no-arbitrage from observable instruments. Barely models at all; model risk is low and mostly about correct discounting curves.
- **Standard options** — the model is a **quoting convention**. Black–Scholes is used not because anyone believes it but because it is a smooth, invertible map from price to implied vol. Everyone knows the assumptions are false; the model is a communication device, and the calibrated surface carries the real information.
- **Exotics and illiquid products** — no market to calibrate to, so the model genuinely determines the price. This is where model risk is severe and where different desks can hold the same trade at materially different marks.

## Physics vs finance
Hull's framing, and a good thing to say out loud: physical laws are stable and can be tested to many decimal places. Financial "laws" describe the behaviour of people who react to the model itself. A model that becomes widely used changes the market it describes — the post-1987 volatility skew is the standard example, appearing only after everyone had adopted Black–Scholes.

## Common failure modes
- **Calibration to a benign window** — parameters estimated in calm markets, used in stressed ones.
- **Overfitting** — enough parameters to fit anything, including the noise.
- **Extrapolation** — a model calibrated to liquid strikes and maturities used far outside that range.
- **Correlation assumptions** — usually the weakest input, and the one that moves most in stress.
- **Implementation bugs** — genuinely a large share of realised losses, and the least glamorous.
- **Marking to model in illiquid markets** — where the P&L is whatever the model says, so a bad model quietly produces fictional profits.

## Detecting problems
- **Backtest** predictions against outcomes, and take exception clustering seriously.
- **P&L attribution** — explain daily P&L by the Greeks; a large unexplained residual is the single best early warning that the model is missing a risk factor. This is exactly why FRTB made it a formal test.
- **Benchmark** against an independent model built differently.
- **Stress the parameters**, not just the market — reprice under plausible alternative calibrations and see how much the value moves. That spread *is* your model risk, and it is what a model reserve should be sized against.
- Watch for a desk that is consistently, inexplicably profitable. That is usually a marking problem, not skill.

## Governance
Independent validation, a model inventory with tiering by materiality, periodic revalidation, and documented limitations. The regulatory anchor is the Fed's **SR 11-7**, whose central idea is worth quoting: validation is not just checking the maths, it is challenging whether the model is fit for the purpose it is actually being used for.

## Common mistakes
- Saying "all models are wrong" and stopping there — name the specific failure mode and how you would detect it.
- Confusing validation (is it the right model?) with verification (is the code correct?).
- Treating a calibrated model as validated. Fitting today's prices says nothing about tomorrow's behaviour.
